title: Adam Grant on How to Vibe
author: David Epstein
summary: David Epstein interviews psychologist Adam Grant about his new book Vibe, on building strong connections in a lonely world. Grant opens by reframing the finding that only about half of the people we call friends call us friends, arguing that the word is too broad and that we need three kinds of relationships: allies who share goals, pals who share interests and companions who share values. The Q&A then covers the strength of weak ties, the idea of if-then signatures that explain why people behave differently in different settings, how often friends really need to be in touch, and why skipping small talk for playful icebreakers works. Grant also explains how respectful disagreement can turn adversaries into friends. A closing lightning round tests folk wisdom on opposites attracting, brutal honesty, the feedback sandwich and class size. The piece is a compact guide to interpersonal skill that applies directly to working with teams.
points: Grant sorts relationships into allies, pals and companions, and suggests clarifying which role each person plays so expectations match.
Distant friends often matter more for opportunity because they know about new openings, a point sociologists call the strength of weak ties.
Noticing someone's if-then signature, for example timid with older siblings but brave with friends, lets you shape the situation to bring out their best.
Skipping small talk for a playful question and telling people you will still care after long silences are practical ways to build and keep bonds.
In the lightning round Grant argues against the feedback sandwich and brutal honesty, recommending direct content delivered with kindness.
quotes: I’ve found that we need three kinds of people: allies, pals, and companions. Allies are people who share our goals: we’re on a mission together.

You’re more likely to get a job through distant friends than close friends. It’s not just due to numbers; the people you don’t know well are more likely to know about new opportunities and open new doors.

Different situations bring out different sides of us. My favorite example is Dwight Schrute on The Office: if he’s with a subordinate, then he’s domineering, but if he’s with a superior, he’s deferential.
Strong bonds can survive months or even years of distance. It’s common, though, for people to mistake a lapse in communication for a lack of care.
Respectful disagreement can bring us closer together—it signals that we care enough about one another’s opinions to put energy into trying to change them.
To paraphrase Bob Burg, people who take pride in being brutally honest are mostly interested in being brutal. Be direct in what you say but kind in how you say it.

It’s time to take the feedback sandwich off the menu; it doesn’t taste as good as it sounds. It’s more effective to just tell people you have comments on areas of both strength and growth and ask which one they want to hear first.
